name: Erik Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead in the transport planning office at a supermarket chain's distribution centre. It's the big grey warehouse by the ring road, and it's most of the jobs in our town. I've got five planners under me who build the delivery routes and slot times for the lorries going out to the stores. I start at six, check overnight problems, take calls from angry store managers, and try to keep the drivers' hours legal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out the most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The phone, mostly. Some days it's forty calls before lunch, and I'm still not great at saying no to the store managers. I got the job a year ago because I'd been a planner for three years and my boss, Henrik, liked that I turned up. I live with my girlfriend Sanne, who works at a bakery, and between the rent and my car loan there's not much left at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I never trusted it anyway. At work I'd say it in the canteen and most people would nod. I don't post online much, maybe a thumbs-up on someone else's post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be worried, just not about AI. Head office already announced a cost review in September, and planning offices are always the first place they look. Even a bit of route software that saves an hour a day could be the excuse to merge us with the depot two hours away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job well, that's the main thing. I'd stop the gym membership and the streaming services to put a bit aside. And I'd ask Henrik straight out what the cost review means for our office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest, even without the AI part. The review is real and it's already happening. I don't sleep great on Sunday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said merging with the other depot. What happens to you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's a two-hour drive each way, or nothing. Sanne won't move, her mum is here and the bakery is the only job she's ever liked. So I'd probably end up back on the warehouse floor if they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever tried the AI tools at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A couple of the younger planners use something on their phones to write emails, but I don't trust what I don't understand. If an AI tool books a lorry to the wrong store, it's my name on the mistake, not the computer's.

say: I'd say good, because I **never trusted** AI anyway.
I'd say it in the **canteen**, not online, where most people would agree.
think: The **cost review** head office announced is still a threat without AI.
Even small route software could justify **merging our office** with the depot two hours away.
do: Keep my head down and **do the job well** to stay safe.
Cancel the **gym and streaming** to put a little aside.
Ask my boss **straight out** what the cost review means for us.
feel: Anxious anyway, with **bad Sunday nights** because of the cost review.
S0.quote: If an AI tool books a lorry to the wrong store, it's my name on the mistake, not the computer's.
fieldNote: He was **already anxious** before AI came up, because of the cost review.
He's never used AI and **distrusts** what he can't check himself.
His fallback is the **warehouse floor**, because his girlfriend won't move.

steps.text: Keep turning up early and doing the routes carefully
Cancel the gym membership and two streaming services
Ask Henrik (his boss) what the cost review means for planning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bosses are rushing it, and someone needs to make sure the lorries still turn up. At work I'd probably grumble with the older planners. I'd keep it practical, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, planning routes and booking slots is exactly what that card describes. If the software does the routes, they need one person to watch it, not five planners and me. And I'm the worst on the team at computers, so I'm not the one they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about moving back to the warehouse floor, picking or forklift, since robots come slower there. I'd sell the car and get something older to kill the loan. And I'd probably wait a bit to see if the software actually works before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I worked three years to get off the warehouse floor, and I'd be asking to go back. Going backwards before I've even started. That's how it feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see if it works. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen two systems come in already that were meant to change everything, and both times we ended up doing it by hand. I'd rather not throw away my job for a system that might not work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, probably. My dad drove for this same company for twenty years. Dad (a retired lorry driver) would tell me to stop moaning and get my forklift licence back up to date.

say: I'd say the bosses are **rushing it** and lorries still need to arrive.
I'd keep it **practical, not political**, grumbling with the older planners.
think: Route planning and slot booking are **exactly** what the card describes.
Software needs one watcher, not five planners, and I'm the **worst at computers**.
do: Ask to move back to **picking or forklift** work on the warehouse floor.
Swap the car for an **older one** to clear the loan.
**Wait and see** if the new software actually works first.
feel: Alarmed and **going backwards**, after three years getting off the floor.
S1.quote: I worked three years to get off the warehouse floor, and I'd be asking to go back. Going backwards before I've even started.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the role** because he's the least tech-minded on the team.
Past failed systems make him want to **wait**, which could cost him time.
His father's **lorry-driving** history pulls him toward hands-on work.

steps.text: Ask Henrik (his boss) about forklift or picking shifts
Swap the car for an older one to clear the loan
Watch whether the new routing software works before deciding more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what anyone's supposed to do with two years. At work I'd probably go quiet. I'm not the type to make speeches about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my planning job's finished in 2028, and the warehouse job I'd fall back to is finished around 2031. I'd be thirty with nothing and no plan. I genuinely don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab whatever hands-on work exists, forklift, loading, anything, just to earn through the three years before robots. I'd move in with my parents to stop paying rent, if Sanne would come. Beyond that, I honestly have nothing, and no money to make a plan with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. My chest goes tight just thinking about it. I'd feel like the floor was going and then the floor under the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sanne come to your parents' house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Her bakery is here, my parents are forty minutes away, and her shifts start at four. We'd probably fight about it, and I'm scared of what that does to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn, even with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I could learn fast enough to beat a machine that learns everything. People keep saying retrain, but retrain into what, when the thinking jobs go first? I'd rather spend the time earning while I can.

say: I'd say I don't know what anyone does with **two years**.
I'd probably **go quiet** at work rather than make speeches.
think: My desk job ends in **2028** and the floor job around **2031**.
I'd be thirty with **no plan** and no money to make one.
do: Grab any **hands-on work** to earn through the three years before robots.
Move in with **my parents** to stop paying rent.
feel: Like losing the floor, then the **floor under the floor**.
S2.quote: My planning job's finished in 2028, and the warehouse job I'd fall back to is finished around 2031. I'd be thirty with nothing and no plan.
fieldNote: He sees the **two-step loss**: desk job first, warehouse job three years later.
With no savings and little appetite for change, he has **no plan**.
Moving home could **strain his relationship** with Sanne.

steps.text: Take any forklift or loading shifts going at the warehouse
Move into his parents' house forty minutes away to cut rent
Ask his parents to help cover bills until work is found

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should get some honest answers from the company about who stays. I'd probably sign the petition if someone else started it. I wouldn't start it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, just with five years. My desk job goes in 2031 and the floor in 2034. Five years is enough to feel it coming but I'm not sure I'd do anything clever with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save some money each month, maybe two hundred, and keep the planning job as long as it lasts. I'd renew my forklift licence and maybe get my lorry licence, because Dad says drivers will be needed until the robots. I'd probably keep hoping it slows down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. It's better than two years, but I keep coming back to the fact that both my jobs go. Sanne says I always expect the worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A lorry licence costs money. Could you afford it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easily. It's about two thousand all in, which is two months of savings I don't have. I'd ask Dad to lend it, which I hate doing at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep hoping it slows down. Do you really think it will?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, if I'm honest. But hoping AI slows down is free and courses aren't. I know that sounds like a cop-out.

say: I'd say the company owes us **honest answers** about who stays.
I'd **sign a petition** if someone else started it, but not start one.
think: My desk job goes in **2031** and the warehouse floor in **2034**.
Five years lets me see it coming, but I doubt I'd **use it well**.
do: Save about **two hundred a month** while keeping the planning job.
Renew my **forklift licence** and try for a lorry licence.
feel: Still **alarmed**, because both his desk job and floor job end.
S3.quote: Hoping AI slows down is free and courses aren't. I know that sounds like a cop-out.
fieldNote: Even five years doesn't calm him, because **both fallback jobs** go.
He admits that **hoping** is easier than paying for training.
Borrowing from **his dad** for a lorry licence feels shameful to him.

steps.text: Put two hundred a month into savings from his pay
Renew his forklift licence and book lorry licence lessons
Borrow about two thousand from his dad for the lorry licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots could change. At work I'd say let's not panic yet. That's what I'd say, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough that I'd probably actually do something. I'd be thirty-seven when the planning job goes and forty when robots hit the floor. That's still young enough to start again, even for someone like me who hates starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the planning job for now, and over two or three years get my lorry licence with savings rather than a loan. I'd probably finally let one of the younger planners show me the AI tools, just so I'm not the only one who can't. And I'd pay off the car before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd sleep better. The cost review still worries me more in the short run than any robot. Ten years feels like a normal amount of time to worry about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let a younger planner show you the tools. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lotte, probably, she's twenty-three and does everything on her phone. Lotte (the youngest planner on my team) would laugh at me for not knowing the AI tools, but kindly. I'd probably bring Lotte a coffee for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about you and Sanne, long term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids, maybe in four or five years. With ten years' warning, I'd want to be settled in something before then. I don't want to be learning to drive a lorry with a baby at home.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long, and lots could change.
I'd tell people at work **not to panic** yet.
think: Ten years is enough that I'd **actually act**, even though I hate starting again.
I'd be **thirty-seven** at AGI and forty when robots reach the floor.
do: Save for a **lorry licence** over two or three years instead of borrowing.
Let a younger planner show me the **AI tools**.
feel: Anxious, but **sleeping better** with ten years.
The **cost review** still worries him more than robots in the short run.
S4.quote: Lotte (the youngest planner on my team) would laugh at me for not knowing the AI tools, but kindly. I'd probably bring Lotte a coffee for it.
fieldNote: Ten years is the first scenario where he'd **try AI tools** at all.
His near-term worry stays the **cost review**, not AI.
He plans around **future children**, wanting to be settled first.

steps.text: Clear the car loan before taking on anything else
Save up and take a lorry licence within three years
Ask Lotte (a junior planner) to show him the route-planning AI

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my desk job and the warehouse job both go and I'd have no time or money to do anything. What would help is something to fall back on while you sort yourself out, like proper pay while you get a licence. And the company being honest early instead of announcing things on a Friday afternoon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that not everyone is a quick learner. People talk like everyone can just retrain, but some of us took three years to get good at one job. A two-year warning doesn't work for people like me.

headlineQuote: People talk like everyone can just retrain, but some of us took three years to get good at one job. A two-year warning doesn't work for people like me.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old transport planning lead** at a supermarket distribution centre that dominates his small town.
He lives with Sanne, a **bakery worker**, with a car loan and almost no savings.
He's pragmatic, **distrusts AI** and has never used it, preferring to wait and see.
A **cost review** already worries him before any AI scenario begins.
Fast AGI leaves him **panicked**, while ten years finally pushes him toward a lorry licence.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both his desk job and warehouse fallback disappear.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid support** while getting a licence or retraining.
The company being **honest early** instead of Friday-afternoon announcements.
